sweep_summary: Both title-works with stress in the title are Florence Gerdel's word-and-phrase pitch-stress study of Páez: the 1985 English chapter (already held by the project; now scanned in full, printed pp.31-42) and its 1983 Spanish twin in Artículos en Lingüística y Campos Afines 12 (SIL archive 18974, 'Not Available Online'; not in HathiTrust/Google Books/archive.org). The 1983 text is nevertheless in hand: the SIL archives listing for pbb (the Internet Archive 2015) turned up Gerdel's 'Fonología del páez (Revisada 1989)' (SIL 19040, 48 pp, downloaded via the Internet Archive), whose note 13 states that its sections 7-8 were published as Gerdel 1983 and Brend 1985:31-42, and whose bibliography lists the two as one work. All three texts agree with the catalog's 'lexical' coding and its deciding quotations (Gerdel 1973:28 'El acento es contrastable..'; Gerdel 1985:32 root-anchoring): stress is contrastive on shape-identical roots, always within the root for non-verbs, medial in trisyllabic roots, and shifted off the root only for Set B verbs under specific suffixes. Refinements from the 1989 revision: the accompanying tone is now called 'ascendente' (rising) rather than 'alto'; the practical orthography writes the accent only on word-final stress and on accented particles (note 30), implying non-final root stress is the unmarked case; the data are from the Pitayó dialect (note 1). Nothing contradicts the classification; no source states a positional default. Recommend adding Gerdel 1989/1990 (SIL 19040) and Gerdel 1983 (as the Spanish version of 1985) to the per-language bibliography. all look-ups were done by direct downloads (Glottolog, SIL record pages, the Internet Archive, archive.org, Fabre).

new_statements.translation: Stress is contrastive and is normally accompanied by rising tone (the acute accent marks this stress-tone): wála 'big', wakú 'tick'; skúutʸh 'wheat', luúts 'child'; séena? 'terrible', meemé? 'it is higuillo'. || The main location of the pitch-stress nucleus is the root. However, when certain suffixes and particles that carry pitch-stress of their own follow a verb root, the phonological nucleus moves away from the verb root. || In a phonological word whose lexical or grammatical root is not a verb, the phonological nucleus, defined by the presence of pitch-stress, is always in the grammatical root.

new_statements.reading: Páez (Pitayó dialect) has one primary stress per phonological word, realised with rising pitch. Its position is lexically contrastive within roots of identical shape (wála/wakú; ísa/wakú; déwe/pedá) and is anchored to the root rather than to a syllable count: non-verb roots always carry it; trisyllabic roots carry it medially; verb roots fall into Set A (stress stays on the root) and Set B (stress moves to the first formative vowel before four tense-aspect suffixes, or to accented allomorphs of five derivational suffixes; otherwise on the root). The 1989 orthography marks the accent only when it is word-final or on an inherently accented particle, so non-final root stress is the unmarked case, but no positional default is stated in any of the three Gerdel texts. This is a lexical/morphologically anchored system, not a positional (penult) one.

new_statements.translation: 3. Accent. A stressed syllable also carries a rising tone. The orthographic accent is written when the last syllable of the word is stressed and also to mark certain particles that are always stressed: wacú 'tick' [...] || In the present and future some verbs show vowel modifications of the root: if the root ends in a vowel, the final vowel is lengthened; if the root ends in a consonant, the formative vowel is lengthened. In both cases the prosodic accent falls on the syllable with the lengthened vowel. [...] When certain other suffixes are added to this type of verb root, the prosodic accent moves off the root and falls on the suffix.

new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the catalog_records rule (Gordon: penultimate, penultimate stress): the grammar has final-stressed words (wacú) and accent on suffixes, and states no positional rule. It agrees with and refines the existing_statement from Gerdel 1990 (same authors' team; the pronunciation section is by Gerdel): adds the orthographic convention (accent written only when final or on inherently accented particles) and the vowel-lengthening verb class. download note: the catalog open_url abstract.asp?id=20108 now returns 404; the current record is SIL archive 18785, whose reapdata PDF is behind an automated-access block JS challenge (not reachable by automated download), so the PDF was taken archive…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stressed syllable per word, realised with rising pitch; its position is not given by a syllable-count rule. The orthography writes the accent only when it is word-final or on the always-stressed particles (-mée negative, vaa probability), so non-final stress is the unmarked case; final-stressed words exist (wacú 'tick', interrogatives with accented final -a'/glottal stop, p.79). In one verb class (Class A roots with a lengthened final/formative vowel, e.g. wetée- 'fall', pacuée- 'seek', uyúu- 'see') the accent sits on the lengthened vowel in present/progressive/future, and moves onto suffixes such as -cajn, -ni, -sa, -nu, -wa'j; this is the Set B behaviour of Gerdel 1985/1990 seen from the grammar side.
new_statements.exceptions: Particles -mée 'negative' and vaa 'probability' always carry accent and rising tone in the phonological phrase (pp.73, 97, footnotes citing Gerdel 1983); accent-bearing suffixes attract the accent off Class A lengthened-vowel roots (p.39); interrogative suffix -a'/final glottal stop with accent and rising tone on the final syllable (p.79).
new_statements.identity_note: All Gerdel/Slocum descriptions rest on the same material: Gerdel and Slocum 1976 p.262 states the data 'represent the Pitayó dialect' (Cauca), gathered 1964-1972 with consultants Porfirio Ocaña Nache and Rogerio Yonda Güejia; Gerdel 1985 n.1 and the Slocum 1986 prologue name the same consultants, so the stress description is of the Pitayó variety of Páez (Nasa Yuwe). Mondelli 2014 (not in the works list) is a phonetic study of one other speaker.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the source of the existing_statement, which it matches exactly (sec. 4 quote verified against the scanned). Against the catalog_records rule (Gordon, penultimate) it disagrees: Gerdel describes a lexically contrastive, root-anchored stress with final-stressed roots (wakú, pedá, meemé?) and morphologically conditioned shifts, not a penultimate default. Note 13 (p.39) says secs. 7 and 8 were published in Gerdel 1983 and in Brend 1985:31-42, so this work also stands in for index 0.
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per phonological word, carried with rising pitch, contrastive in position within roots of the same shape (wála vs wakú; ísa vs iisá; déwe vs déewe; pedá vs piisáa). It is anchored to the root: non-verb roots and Set A verb roots always carry it; trisyllabic roots carry it medially; Set B verb roots lose it to the first formative vowel before four simple tense-aspect suffixes (progressive, hortatory, future, habitual present) or to the accented allomorphs of five derivational suffixes, and otherwise keep it on the root. No syllable-count default is stated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated to exist ('El acento secundario puede también estar presente según sea el número de sílabas en la palabra y su posición dentro de la frase fonológica', p.24) but no placement rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Set B verbs shift the accent to the formative vowel or to accented suffix allomorphs (-sáa, etc.); the accent on the second of two identical vowels is optionally suppressed in a phrase whose phrase-accent falls elsewhere (p.18); phrase-level emotive particles (-mée, -bda/vaa, -yu'x, etc.) always form the phrase nucleus and override word-level placement (sec. 8); trisyllabic roots are never initially or finally stressed.
new_statements.identity_note: All Gerdel/Slocum descriptions rest on the same material: Gerdel and Slocum 1976 p.262 states the data 'represent the Pitayó dialect' (Cauca), gathered 1964-1972 with consultants Porfirio Ocaña Nache and Rogerio Yonda Güejia; Gerdel 1985 n.1 and the Slocum 1986 prologue name the same consultants, so the stress description is of the Pitayó variety of Páez (Nasa Yuwe). Mondelli 2014 (not in the works list) is a phonetic study of one other speaker.

new_statements.quote: The phonological word in Paez is marked by two primary features: (1) potential pause at the boundaries, and (2) a phonological nucleus identified by its bearing primary stress and high pitch. A secondary stress may also be present depending upon the number of syllables in the word and its location in the phonological phrase. [p.31] || Stems of three syllables do not carry stress on the first or last syllable. [p.32] || The principal placement of the pitch-stress nucleus of the phonological word is on the stem. However, when certain affixes and particles which innately carry pitch-stress follow verb stems, the phonological nucleus is shifted away from the stem. [p.42]

new_statements.relation_note: Disagrees with the catalog_records rule (Gordon, penultimate): the placement is stem-anchored and lexically contrastive, with final-stressed disyllables (wakú, iisá, pedá, pagáy) and morphological shifts. Agrees with the existing_statement (Gerdel 1990), of which this is the English original (Gerdel 1990 n.13). One descriptive difference: here the pitch correlate is 'high pitch', in the 1989/1990 Spanish 'tono ascendente' (rising) and in Gerdel 1973 'tono alto'. The Brend volume is only the container; the other five languages in it are not Páez.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Same system as Gerdel 1990 secs. 7-8 (of which this is the English version): one primary stress with high pitch per phonological word, located in the stem for nonverbs and Set A verbs, contrastive in position within monomorphemic stems (kátʲ 'corn' vs skúutʲx 'wheat', ísa 'truth' vs iisá 'each', déwe 'to pay' vs déewe 'to defend oneself', wakú 'tick'), medial in trisyllabic stems; Set B verb stems carry the pitch-stress on the first formative vowel before the progressive, hortatory, future and habitual-present markers, on the accented allomorphs of five derivational affixes, and on the stem elsewhere.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'A secondary stress may also be present depending upon the number of syllables in the word and its location in the phonological phrase' (p.31); no placement rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Set B verbs (sec. 2.3.1-2.3.2); homophonous Set A/Set B forms under other suffixes (sec. 2.3.3); note 7: 'a class of emotive forms which override the word-level rules of pitch-stress placement' analysed as phrase-level particles (sec. 3.2.2.1); phrase nucleus bears extra heavy stress and usually extra high pitch and normally falls on the main verb (sec. 3.2.1).
new_statements.identity_note: All Gerdel/Slocum descriptions rest on the same material: Gerdel and Slocum 1976 p.262 states the data 'represent the Pitayó dialect' (Cauca), gathered 1964-1972 with consultants Porfirio Ocaña Nache and Rogerio Yonda Güejia; Gerdel 1985 n.1 and the Slocum 1986 prologue name the same consultants, so the stress description is of the Pitayó variety of Páez (Nasa Yuwe). Mondelli 2014 (not in the works list) is a phonetic study of one other speaker.

readall_conflicts: The catalog_records rule (Gordon: penultimate, penultimate stress) is contradicted by every primary description opened: Gerdel 1985 (in Brend 1985), Gerdel 1990 (= the 1983 article, per its note 13) and the Gerdel pronunciation section in Slocum 1986 all describe one contrastive stress-with-rising/high-pitch per word whose position is lexically fixed within the root (wála vs wakú, ísa vs iisá, déwe vs déewe; final-stressed disyllables exist) and anchored to the root, with morphologically conditioned shifts onto formative vowels or accented suffix allomorphs in Set B verbs and onto always-accented particles (-mée, vaa); trisyllabic roots are medially stressed. Gerdel 1973 (held by the project, not in the works list) says the same with 'tono alto'. The three Gerdel/Slocum sources agree with one another; the only wording difference is 'high pitch' (1985) vs 'tono ascendente' (1986, 1990). Mondelli 2014 (held by the project from the earlier reading, not in the works list) measured amplitude on 18 disyllabic nouns from one speaker and read the result as weak word-initial stress, which coincides with penultimate for disyllables but is not a placement rule and does not address the root-anchoring or the final-stressed roots.

audit.recode_to: No forced reclassify. After re-reading Díaz Montenegro 2019 ch.5, decide between keeping 'lexical' (non-strict, root-anchored; Gerdel's Pitayó stems ísa/déwe vs wakú/pedá/lawéč are genuinely contrastive, and Munchique verbs are ˈσσ or σˈσ with PFV/IPFV shift) and 'morphological' (root = accentogenic unit, affixes inert, aspect marked by stress shift, nominal roots ~98% initial in Munchique). Either way add Díaz 2019:201-213 and Mondelli 2014:28-30 as sources and note the dialect difference (Pitayó vs Munchique). Gordon 2002 'Penult' stays contradicted at word level (kíwe-ga 100, ˈstela=aˀs, ˈkiwa=tʲi), though Gerdel 1985:32 'stems of three syllables do not carry stress on the first or last syllable' plus the disyllabic initial default is probably where a stem-level penult reading came from -- worth saying in the contra note.

[p.24] || En una palabra fonológica en la cual la raíz léxica o gramatical no es un verbo, el núcleo fonológico, definido por la presencia de tono-acento, está siempre en la raíz gramatical. [p.25]

sources.quote: 3. El acento. Una sílaba acentuada lleva a su vez un tono ascendente. Se escribe el acento ortográfico cuando la última sílaba de la palabra está acentuada y también para indicar ciertas partículas que son siempre acentuadas: wacú garrapata [...] [p. vi] || En el presente y futuro algunos verbos presentan modificaciones vocálicas de la raíz: si la raíz termina en vocal, se alarga la vocal final; si la raíz termina en consonante, se alarga la vocal formativa. En ambos casos, el acento prosódico recae sobre la sílaba con vocal alargada. Against the catalog_records rule (Gordon, penultimate) it disagrees: Gerdel describes a lexically contrastive, root-anchored stress with final-stressed roots (wakú, pedá, meemé?) and morphologically conditioned shifts, not a penultimate default. sources.quote: The phonological word in Paez is marked by two primary features: (1) potential pause at the boundaries, and (2) a phonological nucleus identified by its bearing primary stress and high pitch. A secondary stress may also be present depending upon the number of syllables in the word and its location in the phonological phrase. [p.31] || Stems of three syllables do not carry stress on the first or last syllable. [p.32] || The principal placement of the pitch-stress nucleus of the phonological word is on the stem. However, when certain affixes and particles which innately carry pitch-stress follow verb stems, the phonological nucleus is shifted away from the stem. [p.42]
sources.locator: Gerdel, Florence L., 'Páez: Pitch and stress in the phonological word and phrase', printed pp.31-42 (PDF 37-48): sec. 2 p.31, sec. 2.1 p.32, secs. 2.2-2.3.3 pp.32-34, sec. 5 Summary p.42, notes 4-7 p.42
sources.note: Disagrees with the catalog_records rule (Gordon, penultimate): the placement is stem-anchored and lexically contrastive, with final-stressed disyllables (wakú, iisá, pedá, pagáy) and morphological shifts. Agrees with the existing_statement (Gerdel 1990), of which this is the English original (Gerdel 1990 n.13). One descriptive difference: here the pitch correlate is 'high pitch', in the 1989/1990 Spanish 'tono ascendente' (rising) and in Gerdel 1973 'tono alto'. The Brend volume is only the container; the other five languages in it are not Páez.
